source_text: Τί γὰρ ἔχεις, φησὶν, ὃ οὐκ ἔλαβες; εἰ δὲ καὶ ἔλαβες, τί καυχᾶσαι ὡς μὴ λαβών; Ἐβουλόμην μὲν πρῶτον ἁπάντων εἰπεῖν· Τί δήποτε παραδραμόντες ἡμῶν οἱ πατέρες ἅπαντα τὸν ἐνιαυτὸν, ἐν τούτῳ τῷ καιρῷ μυσταγωγεῖσθαι τὰ τέκνα τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἐνομοθέτησαν; καὶ τίνος ἕνεκεν μετὰ τὴν παρ' ἡμῶν διδασκαλίαν ὑπολύσαντες ὑμᾶς καὶ ἀποδύσαντες, γυμνοὺς καὶ ἀνυποδέτους μετὰ τοῦ χιτωνίσκου μόνου πρὸς τὰς τῶν ἐξορκιζόντων παραπέμπουσι φωνάς. Οὐ γὰρ ἁπλῶς οὐδὲ εἰκῆ καὶ τὸ σχῆμα καὶ τὸν καιρὸν ἐκεῖνοι τοῦτον ἡμῖν διετύπωσαν· ἀλλ' ἔχει ταῦτα ἀμφότερα μυστικόν τινα λόγον καὶ ἀπόῤῥητον. Καὶ τοῦτον ὑμῖν ἐβουλόμην εἰπεῖν· ὁρῶ δὲ ὅτι πρὸς ἕτερον ἀναγκαιότερον ἡμᾶς κατεπείγει νῦν ὁ λόγος. Ἀνάγκη γὰρ εἰπεῖν τί ποτέ ἐστι τὸ βάπτισμα, καὶ τίνος ἕνεκεν εἰς τὸν βίον εἰσῆλθε τὸν ἡμέτερον, καὶ πόσα κομίζει ἡμῖν τὰ ἀγαθά. Ἀλλ', εἰ βούλεσθε, πρότερον περὶ τῆς προσηγορίας τοῦ μυστικοῦ τούτου καθαρμοῦ διαλεχθῶμεν. Οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἓν αὐτῷ ὄνομα, ἀλλὰ πολλὰ καὶ παντοδαπά· τὸ γὰρ καθάρσιον τοῦτο καλεῖται λουτρὸν παλιγγενεσίας· Ἔσωσε γὰρ ἡμᾶς, φησὶ, διὰ λουτροῦ παλιγγενεσίας καὶ ἀνακαινίσεως Πνεύματος ἁγίου. Καλεῖται καὶ φώτισμα, καὶ τοῦτο Παῦλος αὐτὸ πάλιν ἐκάλεσεν· Ἀναμιμνήσκεσθε γὰρ τὰς πρότερον ἡμέρας, ἐν αἷς φωτισθέντες πολλὴν ἄθλησιν ὑπεμείνατε παθημάτων· καὶ πάλιν, Ἀδύνατον γὰρ τοὺς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας καὶ γευσαμένους τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς ἐπουρανίου, καὶ παραπεσόντας, πάλιν ἀνακαινίζειν εἰς μετάνοιαν. Καλεῖται καὶ βάπτισμα· Ὅσοι γὰρ εἰς Χριστὸν ἐβαπτίσθητε, Χριστὸν ἐνεδύσασθε. Καλεῖται ταφή· Συνετάφητε γὰρ αὐτῷ, φησὶ, διὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος εἰς τὸν θάνατον. Καλεῖται περιτομή· Ἐν ᾧ καὶ περιετμήθητε περιτομῇ ἀχειροποιήτῳ, ἐν τῇ ἀπεκδύσει τοῦ σώματος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τῆς σαρκός. Καλεῖται σταυρός· Ὁ παλαιὸς γὰρ ἄνθρωπος ἡμῶν συνεσταυρώθη, ἵνα καταργηθῇ τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἁμαρτίας. Ἔστι καὶ ἕτερα πλείονα τούτων εἰπεῖν ὀνόματα, ἀλλ' ἵνα μὴ τὸν καιρὸν ἅπαντα εἰς τὰς προσηγορίας τοῦ χαρίσματος ἀνα49.226 λώσωμεν, φέρε ἐπὶ τὴν προτέραν προσηγορίαν ἐλθόντες, καὶ ταύτης τὴν σημασίαν εἰπόντες καταπαύσωμεν τὸν λόγον· τέως δὲ ἀνωτέρω μικρὸν τὴν διδασκαλίαν ἑλκύσωμεν. Ἔστι τὸ κοινὸν ἁπάντων ἀνθρώπων λουτρὸν τὸ διὰ τῶν βαλανείων, ὃ τὸν τοῦ σώματος ἀποσμήχειν εἴωθε ῥύπον· ἔστι δὲ καὶ λουτρὸν Ἰουδαϊκὸν, ἐκείνου μὲν σεμνότερον, τοῦ δὲ τῆς χάριτος πολὺ κατώτερον· καὶ αὐτὸ μὲν γὰρ σωματικὸν ἀποσμήχει ῥύπον, ἀλλ' οὐχ ἁπλῶς σωματικὸν, ἀλλὰ καὶ συνειδότος ἁπτόμενον ἀσθενοῦς. Ἔστι γὰρ πολλὰ τῶν πραγμάτων, ἃ φύσει μὲν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀκάθαρτα, ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς ἀσθενείας τοῦ συνειδότος ἀκάθαρτα γίνεται. Καὶ καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν παιδίων τὰ προσωπεῖα καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ μορμολύκεια φύσει μὲν οὐκ ἔστι φοβερὰ, φοβερὰ δὲ εἶναι τοῖς παιδίοις δοκεῖ διὰ τὴν τῆς φύσεως ἀσθένειαν, οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τούτων ὧν εἶπον· οἷον τὸ νεκρῶν ἅψασθαι σωμάτων, φύσει μὲν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀκάθαρτον, ὅταν δὲ ἀσθενοῦς ἐπιλάβηται συνειδότος, ἀκάθαρτον ποιεῖ τὸν ἁψάμενον. Ὅτι γὰρ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀκάθαρτον φύσει τὸ πρᾶγμα, αὐτὸς ὁ ταῦτα διαταξάμενος Μωϋσῆς ἐδήλωσεν, ὁλόκληρον ἐπιφερόμενος μεθ' ἑαυτοῦ νεκρὸν τὸν Ἰωσὴφ, καὶ μένων καθαρός. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ Παῦλος ἡμῖν περὶ τῆς ἀκαθαρσίας ταύτης διαλεγόμενος τῆς οὐ φύσει γινομένης, ἀλλὰ δι' ἀσθένειαν τοῦ συνειδότος, οὑτωσί πώς φησιν· Οὐδὲν κοινὸν δι' ἑαυτοῦ, εἰ μὴ τῷ λογιζομένῳ τι κοινὸν εἶναι.
orientation: John Chrysostom is addressing the catechumens preparing for baptism, and he now turns to explain what baptism itself is and why it entered human life.
pass_a_gloss: For what do you have, he says, that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? I wanted first of all to say: Why in the world did our fathers, passing over the whole year, ordain that the children of the Church be initiated at this season? And for what reason, after the teaching from us, do they loosen you and strip you, and send you on barefoot and naked with only a tunic to the voices of the exorcists? For not simply nor at random did they prescribe for us this form and this season; but both of these have some mystical and secret reason. And this I wanted to tell you; but I see that the discourse now presses us toward another more necessary matter. For it is necessary to say what baptism ever is, and for what reason it entered into our life, and how many good things it brings us. But, if you wish, let us first discuss the name of this mystical purification. For it does not have one name, but many and of every kind; for this cleansing is called washing of regeneration; For he saved us, he says, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. It is also called enlightenment, and this Paul himself again called it; For recall the earlier days, in which after being enlightened you endured a great contest of sufferings; and again, For it is impossible for those once enlightened and having tasted the heavenly gift, and having fallen away, to renew them again to repentance. It is also called baptism; For as many of you as were baptized into Christ, you put on Christ. It is called burial; For you were buried with him, he says, through baptism into death. It is called circumcision; In whom also you were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping off of the body of the sins of the flesh. It is called cross; For our old man was crucified with him, in order that the body of sin might be destroyed. It is possible to say still more names than these, but in order that we may not spend the whole season on the names of the gift, come, let us go to the first name, and having said its meaning let us bring the discourse to rest; but for now let us draw the teaching up a little higher. There is the common bath of all human beings, the one through the bathhouses, which is accustomed to wipe away the filth of the body; and there is also the Jewish bath, more solemn than that one, but far inferior to the bath of grace; for it too wipes away bodily filth, but not simply bodily filth, but also touching a weak conscience. For there are many things which are not unclean by nature, but become unclean from the weakness of the conscience. And just as in the case of children, masks and the other bogeymen are not fearful by nature, but seem to children to be fearful because of the weakness of their nature, so also in the case of these things which I mentioned; for example, touching dead bodies is not unclean by nature, but whenever it takes hold of a weak conscience, it makes the one who touched unclean. For that the matter is not unclean by nature, Moses himself who ordained these things made clear, carrying with himself the whole dead body of Joseph, and remaining clean. For this reason Paul too, discussing with us this uncleanness which does not come about by nature but through weakness of conscience, says somehow in this way: Nothing is common through itself, except to the one who reckons something to be common.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for baptism as complete re-creation; must be used exactly.
Fixed glossary term for baptism as enlightenment.
Glossary gives 'initiation' for μυσταγωγία; the verb here means to receive that initiation.
rejected: to be led into the mysteries

choices.why: Keeps the physical scrubbing sense of the bathhouse image, distinct from the spiritual cleansing.
Paul's technical term for ritually unclean; 'common' preserves the literal sense and the Pauline usage.
Concrete term for children's frightening figures, matching the mask imagery.

pass_b_english: For what do you have, Paul says, that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not? (1 Corinthians 4:7). I wanted first of all to say: Why did our fathers pass over the whole year and ordain that the children of the Church be initiated at this season? And why, after our instruction, do they loosen your sandals and strip off your clothes, and send you barefoot and wearing only a tunic to the voices of those who exorcize? For they did not design this posture and this season for us simply or at random; both of these things hold a mystical and ineffable meaning. And I wanted to tell you this meaning. But I see that the argument now presses us toward something more necessary. For I must say what baptism is, and why it entered our life, and how many good things it brings us.

But if you wish, let us first discuss the name of this mystical cleansing. For it does not have one name, but many and varied. This purification is called the washing of regeneration: He saved us, Paul says, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5). It is also called enlightenment, and Paul himself called it this as well: Remember the earlier days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a great struggle of sufferings (Hebrews 10:32); and again: For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened and tasted the heavenly gift, and then fell away, to be renewed again to repentance (Hebrews 6:4-6). It is also called baptism: For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ (Galatians 3:27). It is called burial: You were buried with him, Paul says, through baptism into death (Romans 6:4). It is called circumcision: In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping off of the body of the sins of the flesh (Colossians 2:11). It is called cross: Our old self was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be brought to nothing (Romans 6:6). There are many other names I could mention besides these, but so that we do not spend the whole time on the titles of the gift, let us come to the first title, explain its meaning, and bring the discussion to rest. But first let us draw the teaching back a little.

There is a washing common to all people, the washing in the bathhouses, which is accustomed to wipe away the filth of the body. There is also a Jewish washing, more solemn than that one, but far inferior to the washing of grace. For it too wipes away bodily filth, but not simply bodily filth—it also touches a weak conscience. For there are many things that are not unclean by nature, but become unclean from the weakness of the conscience. And just as with children, masks and other bogeymen are not frightening by nature, but seem frightening to children because of the weakness of their nature, so it is with the things I mentioned. For example, touching dead bodies is not unclean by nature, but when it takes hold of a weak conscience, it makes the one who touches unclean. That the thing is not unclean by nature, Moses himself—the very one who ordained these things—made clear, for he carried with himself the whole corpse of Joseph and remained clean. For this reason Paul, speaking to us about this uncleanness that does not come by nature but through weakness of conscience, says something like this: Nothing is common in itself, except to the one who considers something common (Romans 14:14).

last_rejected.source_quote: Ἀδύνατον γὰρ τοὺς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας καὶ γευσαμένους τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς ἐπουρανίου, καὶ παραπεσόντας, πάλιν ἀνακαινίζειν εἰς μετάνοιαν
last_rejected.why: The source quotes only Hebrews 6:4, not 6:4-6; it stops at πάλιν ἀνακαινίζειν εἰς μετάνοιαν (Heb 6:6a), not the full verses 4-6.
last_rejected.ruling: Source quotes Heb 6:4-6a continuously; citing 6:4-6 is standard shorthand, not misleading.

last_rejected.why: ἐνομοθέτησαν means 'made a law/legislated', not 'ordain' in the ecclesiastical sense; 'ordain' suggests sacramental ordination, misleading.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐνομοθέτησαν means 'enacted/ordained as law'; 'ordain' here means 'establish,' not sacramental ordination.

last_rejected.why: ὑπολύσαντες means 'causing you to take off/loosen' your own sandals, not 'they loosen your sandals'; agency is wrong.
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπολύσαντες ὑμᾶς naturally means 'loosening your sandals'; causative agency is implicit and not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: stripping off of the body of the sins of the flesh
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐν τῇ ἀπεκδύσει τοῦ σώματος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τῆς σαρκός
last_rejected.why: ἀπεκδύσει means 'stripping off/putting off' (the body of sins), not 'stripping off of the body'; the genitive chain is misread.
last_rejected.fix: in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh
last_rejected.ruling: ἀπεκδύσει governs σώματος; 'stripping off of the body of sins' follows the genitive chain correctly per Col 2:11.

last_rejected.why: καταργηθῇ means 'destroyed, rendered powerless, abolished', not merely 'brought to nothing'; the body of sin is to be destroyed.
last_rejected.ruling: καταργηθῇ includes 'brought to nothing'; 'destroyed' is a preference, not a meaning change.
